name.text: Exploring data: Kenyan schools (six visual discoveries)

questiontext.text:
Exploring a survey of Kenyan schools

Imagine that a research team has visited 60 schools in six Kenyan counties. They record details

  • at the student level, such as the students' reading and mathematics assessment scores
  • at the classroom level, such as the classroom size.
  • at the school level, such as if the school is in an urban or rural setting, or if it is primary or secondary.
They calculate the average reading and mathematics scores for each school, and so have that information now at the school level. Similarly, they average the classroom size by school, and so have the typical classroom size per school.

In other words, this data is at the school level: Each data point is one school, and the variables they have are the school's average reading and mathematics assessment scores, typical class size, school type, and whether it is in an urban or rural setting. The team wants to understand what the schools have in common, how they differ and which questions are worth investigating further.

Your role is to explore the school-level data. Build plots to investigate the researchers' questions, then use what you see to answer. You do not need to calculate anything or write code. These are synthetic teaching data, not measurements from actual Kenyan schools. This means that each time you generate this question, you get new data, and hence this question can be answered as many times as you want.

Do reading and mathematics results go together?

One question the researchers are interested in is how do reading scores change as mathematics scores increase? Create a scatterplot and choose the description that best fits the schools in this survey.

2. Is there one typical reading score?

Each school has an average reading score. We can look at the spread of these reading scores by looking at a boxplot, or a histogram. Both can give different insights. The researchers wish to explore if the average reading scores are fairly evenly spread across all the schools, or if there are unusually low or high scores stretching one side of the distribution.

Start with the boxplot: What does it suggest about the spread of reading scores across the schools?

[[input:ans_shape]] [[validation:ans_shape]]

Now, look at the histogram. This is another way to view the same reading scores: each bar shows how many schools fall within a range of scores. What does this suggest about the schools' reading scores?

[[input:ans_peaks]] [[validation:ans_peaks]]

The researchers wish to compare reading scores at primary and secondary schools.

Which school type has the higher median reading score in this survey?

[[input:ans_overlap]] [[validation:ans_overlap]]

generalfeedback.text:
What these plots teach us

Scatterplots: A positive relationship rises as X increases; a negative one falls. A linear relationship can be approximated by a straight line, even if the observations do not lie exactly on it. No apparent relationship means no clear overall upward or downward pattern.

Boxplots and histograms: A roughly symmetric distribution has balanced left and right sides. Left-skew has a longer tail towards smaller values; right-skew has a longer tail towards larger values. The reading-score data are approximately symmetric but contain two moderately separated clusters. The boxplot can conceal these clusters; the histogram begins at bin width 8. Try narrower and wider bins to see how the two concentrations become more or less visible.

Bar charts: A bar chart compares frequencies of categories. Here the counties refer only to the synthetic sample, not to real county-wide school totals.

Filtering: Selecting urban or rural schools displays a subset of the same dataset; it does not change their measurements. This is an introductory demonstration of filtering, not an inference about actual Kenyan schools.

Grouped boxplots: Compare medians and overlap separately. A higher median does not mean that every school in one group has a higher score than every school in the other.

Axis scales: Changing axis limits changes how a relationship looks, but does not change the observations.
